headline: Fertilizer feeds billions and chokes the Gulf

portrait.alt: Etched profile portrait of Fritz Haber, bald, with round glasses
portrait.credit: Fritz Haber, etching by Emil Orlik, 1922. Public domain.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: Fertilizer was running short
slides.text: Crops need nitrogen. Around 1900 most came from bird droppings and mined saltpeter, and **a chemist warned the world would run short of wheat.**
slides.alt: Workers loading guano into a rail cart at the foot of a huge pale heap, Chincha Islands, Peru, 1865
slides.credit: Guano mining, Chincha Islands, Peru, 1865. Henry de Witt Moulton. Public domain.

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: Ammonia out of thin air
slides.text: In 1909 Fritz Haber made ammonia from the nitrogen in air, and Carl Bosch scaled it up. **One estimate: it fed 48% of the world in 2008.**
slides.alt: A combine harvesting a vast golden wheat field on rolling hills
slides.credit: Wheat harvest on the Palouse. USDA. Public domain.

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: Runoff feeds a dead zone
slides.statLabel: square miles of Gulf of Mexico dead zone in summer 2025, per NOAA
slides.text: The nitrogen crops don't take up washes downriver and feeds algae. **Each summer the Gulf of Mexico gets a dead zone.**
slides.alt: Satellite view of brown and green water spreading from the Louisiana coast into the deep blue Gulf of Mexico
slides.credit: Sediment and phytoplankton in the Gulf of Mexico, 2023. NASA. Public domain.

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: War, yes. Rivers, no.
slides.text: The harm to rivers, coasts and climate showed up once fertilizer use had grown many times over. **A 2008 review says Haber could not foresee it.**

slides.label: The long cleanup
slides.title: Same process, same dead zone
slides.text: The process has barely changed since 1913. **The Gulf dead zone still averages more than twice its 2035 target.**

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: Food for 48% of the world's people in 2008, one estimate finds
People fed per hectare: 1.9 in 1908, 4.3 in 2008 (same study)
No more depending on mined bird droppings and saltpeter
costs: Nitric acid for German explosives in World War I
A Gulf of Mexico dead zone of 4,402 square miles, summer 2025 (NOAA)
Farming: 74% of human-made nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas, in the 2010s
slides.text: It feeds about half the world, one estimate finds. **The extra nitrogen ends up in rivers, sea and air.**

slides.label: Pattern
slides.title: Solve a shortage, create a surplus
slides.text: Once nitrogen was cheap, farms could spread more than crops take up. **The shortage ended, and the surplus went downstream.**

slides.label: Lesson
slides.title: When something gets cheap, plan for the extra
slides.text: A fix for too little can quietly become a source of too much. **When something gets cheap, plan for the extra.**
